articles.title: U.S. oil giant Chevron confirms it will expand operations in Venezuela
articles.summary: Chevron plans to invest more than $7 billion over the next five years, with the goal of more than doubling its current production to about 600,000 barrels a day.
articles.body: Oil giant Chevron confirmed that it will expand operations in Venezuela after President Donald Trump announced an ambitious deal to develop the nation’s oil reserves and give the Pentagon a stake in the profits. Chevron, the only U.S. oil company with a major presence in Venezuela, said Wednesday that it has been assigned additional acreage in the Orinoco Belt, where it has active operations. The company plans to invest more than $7 billion over the next five years, with the goal of more than doubling its current production to about 600,000 barrels a day. “Chevron’s history in Venezuela spans more than a century, and our expanded position reflects our confidence in the country’s deep resource potential,” CEO Mike Wirth said in a prepared statement. Venezuela holds the world’s largest proven reserves, totaling more than 303 billion barrels of crude oil, according to OPEC’s 2025 Annual Statistical Bulletin. Saudi Arabia is a distant second with 267 billion barrels. Yet because Venezuela’s energy infrastructure is severely degraded and the nation is operating under international sanctions, its daily production is just over 1 million barrels, compared with the 10 million to 11 million barrels that Saudi Arabia produces each day. The U.S. produces almost 14 million barrels per day. Chevron’s expansion follows U.S. deal with Venezuela Chevron, the second-largest U.S. oil company, has had a presence in Venezuela since 1923. U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright on Wednesday attended a ceremony in Venezuela’s capital in which Chevron, Italian oil company Eni and other energy companies signed agreements with the South American country’s government. “President Trump’s mission in Venezuela is straightforward. The mission is to bring peace, freedom, opportunity and prosperity to the people of Venezuela,” Wright said in Caracas. “I believe the deals that are signed today — tens of billions of dollars of investment, ultimately many thousands of jobs — are critical in starting this ball rolling of peace, opportunity and prosperity for everyone in Venezuela.” The White House confirmed Monday that it is partnering with North American Blue Energy Partners, NABEP, as part of Trump’s push to tap into Venezuela’s oil industry. Yet the agreement has been met with skepticism from energy experts who say it will take years to revive Venezuela’s oil industry, which is in disarray after years of neglect. There are also questions about whether Venezuela’s acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, has the authority to give NABEP 100-year rights over 17 oil fields with reserves of 65 billion barrels — and whether future Venezuelan or American administrations would overturn the agreement. U.S. pushes back on criticism Venezuela’s constitution states that arrangements like the one that the United States has entered must be approved by the National Assembly, which has not happened, wrote Ian Vásquez, vice president for international studies at the Cato Institute. “The deal lacks legitimacy since it was agreed to with a dictatorship that has clung to power for decades through violence and by committing what was probably the largest electoral fraud in Latin American history in 2024,” Vásquez wrote. “The agreement was also reached under overwhelming pressure, military and otherwise, from the United States. As such, any future Venezuelan democracy will question the deal, thus undermining confidence in the current arrangement.” The ruling party-controlled National Assembly expressed support for the agreement during its Tuesday session, but lawmakers held no debate or voted to approve it. Wright on Wednesday pushed back on criticism, telling reporters that the deal is “a massive win” for both countries. “Because what it’s going to do is take resources that are underground, not helping anyone, and invest capital and money and technology and bring them to the surface to better the lives of Venezuelans, better supply energy to Americans,” Wright said during a joint press conference with Rodríguez. Trump has eyed Venezuela’s oil since the January capture of then-President Nicolás Maduro and has pressed to get U.S. businesses back into the country. “We have Exxon going in, we have Chevron going in. We have our big oil companies going in,” he said that same month. He suggested again on Monday that other U.S. oil majors were preparing for a return, though other than Chevron, there is no evidence of that. Exxon Mobil CEO Darren Woods said in January that Venezuela was “uninvestable.” An Exxon spokesman said this week that “nothing has changed.” U.S. oil majors remain hesitant The history of U.S. oil majors in Venezuela explains the hesitation. Venezuela nationalized its oil industry in 1976 and created the state-owned company Petróleos de Venezuela S.A. A second nationalization occurred in 2007, when President Hugo Chávez pushed foreign oil companies into state-controlled joint ventures and seized the assets of companies that refused. Chevron agreed to a joint venture. Others, including Exxon and ConocoPhillips, refused, and Venezuela took their assets. Trump has said that the agreement with Venezuela would “substantially lower” gasoline prices in the U.S. However, analysts have repeatedly warned that Venezuela’s dilapidated oil infrastructure will require years of restoration work and tens of billions of dollars to resuscitate. “It could take 2 to 4 years to get new greenfield facilities online in the Orinoco region,” Amy Jaffe, director of the Global Energy, Climate, and Sustainability Lab at New York University, said in an email. “Other places where there is no pipeline and other kinds of support infrastructure could take longer.” Meanwhile, the national average price for a gallon of regular gasoline jumped overnight to $4.12, according to the motor club AAA. That is 93 cents more than it cost at this point last year.

articles.title: With Japan tightening rules for foreign residents, some wonder if it’s time to say ‘sayonara’
articles.summary: Only 3.4% of Japan’s population is immigrants. But tougher rules and higher fees are making it even more difficult for foreigners to obtain residency.
articles.body: Zen gardens, futuristic cityscapes and a vibrant food scene, combined with a favorable exchange rate against the yen, have turned Japan into a tourist magnet that has been drawing in record numbers of visitors in recent years. The number of people settling down for longer-term stays, including work and study, also hit an all-time high last year, likely due to the reliable safety and convenient infrastructure the world’s fourth-largest economy has to offer. But recently, a series of tightened immigration policies imposed by the government has made those who’ve come to call Japan their second home wonder: Is it time to say “sayonara”? Japan has a long history of strict immigration policies and a homogeneous population. However, gripped by a spiraling demographic crisis, the country gradually opened up to foreign workers as well as seeking more international tourists. But such efforts did not wholly succeed. Overtourism and reports — some true, others misconceived — of foreign residents flouting local rules have recently fueled the rise of “Japan-first” politics and reshaped the trajectory of what was becoming a more open, diverse and welcoming society. Last month, the Japanese government, led by conservative Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, said that a range of visa fees would rise in October — the latest in a series of stricter measures for foreigners. Under the new rules, those looking to settle permanently in Japan will have to fork out 20 times more — 200,000 yen ($1,257) — to become a permanent resident. Prices for other work and student visas will also rise. The purpose of the spike in fees is to forge “an orderly society in which foreigners and Japanese citizens coexist,” said Justice Minister Hiroshi Hiraguchi. That left some foreign residents in Japan worrying whether it’s the start of a trend of tougher policies for newcomers. The people in the crosshairs The most drastic shifts impact those who plan to stay in Japan for the longest – those applying for permanent residency, a status that grants rights to work, unlimited entries, and infinite stay. Effective from October, applicants are required to have an income level higher than that of average Japanese households. And from next April, aspiring permanent residents need to have a projected pension fund equivalent to 30 years of payouts. They also have to speak intermediate-level Japanese. “Considering that permanent resident is the most stable status of residence, this revision makes necessary updates to the application of independent livelihood and national interest requirements to ensure applicants do not become a public burden,” said Hiraguchi during a press conference last month. Earlier this year, the government also tightened rules for foreign business owners, raising the capital requirement of a business manager visa popular among entrepreneurs from five million yen ($31,000) to 30 million ($126,000). An impossible balance The number of foreign residents recached 4.1 million last year, a record high representing about 3.4% of the Japanese population. More than 930,000 Chinese nationals live in Japan, making it the largest group, while about 70,000 Americans also reside there. The recent changes followed reports that some foreign residents had been driving up home prices or evading payments for their public health insurance. Japan has a national healthcare system which requires every resident to pay a monthly or yearly fee in order to access discounted medical services. Others have been accused of exploiting the relatively affordable policies to acquire residency by creating shell companies, prompting calls to plug loopholes. A surge in tourists has also annoyed some locals, who’ve accused them of causing a nuisance and increasing the cost of living– problems political pundits say were sometimes wrongly attributed to foreign residents. The anger fueled the rise of Sanseito, a minor right-wing party that rallied against immigrants in recent elections, putting pressure on the ruling Liberal Democratic Party government. But the government’s new policies have sparked concerns among foreigners who have built a life in the country. Some business owners have complained that the new capital requirement, which surged sixfold, significantly reduced their cash flow, rendering their business unsustainable. Many Indian and Nepali restaurants were reportedly forced to close after their owners — most of whom came from their native countries to seek business opportunities in Japan — said their visa renewals had been rejected. One of those affected by the new regulations is a transgender teacher from the US, who asked CNN for anonymity, fearing it could jeopardize her immigration status. Although she and her American spouse have been living in Japan for nearly 10 years and she speaks fluent Japanese, she told CNN that her plans-in-progress to become a permanent resident are now more challenging. “Our long-term goal is always to gain permanent residency, and that in particular is outrageously expensive under the currently proposed guidelines,” she said. “Obviously, it’s something that we could save up for, but it’s a wholly unpredicted expense.” Her gender identity also adds levels of difficulty. Currently, her passport identifies her as a man and she is married to a woman. She can’t change it because Japan doesn’t recognize same-sex marriage. That would eliminate the possibility of using a spousal visa in Japan, which would have provided a backup option to staying in the country should her current work visa fall through. Tokyo-based immigration lawyer Kazuki Yuda, from Touch Immigration Law Firm, said inquiries had spiked recently as people rushed to file their applications before the new changes came in. He said the new rules were too strict and he expected the number of people qualifying for permanent residency to drastically drop. Takaichi’s government is walking a fine line between the need to calm public anger, on which its political foes ride, while addressing the urgent need to replenish the country’s workforce, at a time when its neighbors, from South Korea to Singapore, are loosening rules to attract young talent. Japan’s fertility rate — the average number of children a woman is expected to have during her lifetime — plunged to the lowest in a decade last year at 1.14, although there appeared to be a slight uptick in the first half of this year, according to official statistics. A fertility rate of at least 2.1 is required to maintain a stable population without immigration. As a result, Japan finds itself in a precarious position, caught between a lack of locals to fill roles in the workforce and a distrust of immigrants who can provide labor. For some, Japan was already losing its appeal as a destination for work, as the yen fell to 40-year lows against the dollar. Now worries about visa costs and the uncertainties are causing some to think twice. “As a fresh graduate, fees like this would have been impossible for me. Even now, I’m barely scraping by,” a foreign student wrote on X. “Looking at the Japanese market 10 years from now, I genuinely feel from the bottom of my heart that things are heading for serious trouble,” she wrote.

articles.title: Chris Mason: Reform face headwinds as they gather for conference
articles.summary: The party's continued prominence has brought what prominence always brings: scrutiny, says BBC political editor Chris Mason.
articles.body:
Reform UK begin their annual conference in Birmingham a bigger party than they were a year ago, their numbers swelled at Westminster, at Holyrood, in the Senedd and in local authorities.

But they also gather amid significant political headwinds, much of which revolve around money.

There was that whopping £5m gift to Nigel Farage from Christopher Harborne, the Thailand based British billionaire, and the long running row about whether the money should have been declared by Farage once he became an MP.

Then there is, among other things, the Metropolitan Police investigation into donations to the party during the last general election campaign.

Reform insists that it "takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations."

When the party got together in the same West Midlands venue a year ago, they were an insurgency provoking intrigue and attention and demonstrating plenty of momentum.

Indeed that momentum was so significant that it was a major factor, perhaps the major factor, in accelerating the demise of Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister, because the potential prospect of a Reform government frightened the Labour Party to its core.

Would Starmer, its then desperately unpopular leader, help or hinder their attempts to take on Farage? Hinder was the eventually overwhelming view within Labour, and so Starmer was a goner.

But politics can change, and change quickly. With Starmer out and Burnham in, there is early evidence of some support for Labour picking up. No longer are Reform comfortably leading in all the opinion polls - in some they're not leading at all. Add to this a more confident and prominent Kemi Badenoch leading the Conservatives and the recent rise too of Restore Britain, the outfit set up by the former Reform MP Rupert Lowe. And the Scottish National Party and Plaid Cymru won and so beat them in the devolved elections in Scotland and Wales respectively. In other words, collectively Reform's opponents appear more energised and popular.

Make no mistake, no party at a UK wide level is popular at the moment, but the scrap appears more evenly matched than it did.

Into that mix, Reform's continued prominence has brought what prominence always brings: scrutiny. Nigel Farage is a candidate for prime minister; his senior team candidates for the great offices of state.

When I interviewed Farage at Reform HQ yesterday, on the specifics of the £5m gift and the police investigation he maintained they've acted appropriately.

But he offered an insight into how he perceives the hurricane of questions he faces.

"I think what you're seeing is the establishment - in a very coordinated way - fighting back," he claimed.

I suggested he sounded like a conspiracy theorist, implying the whole world was out to get him.

His answer was instructive: "When you read in the newspaper you're under investigation, and you don't even know a complaint's been made, you can see the degree of collusion that has gone on between interested parties. This will not stop. They will continually try and do this to us."

Who's they? I pressed. He mentioned the House of Commons and House of Lords – full of his political opponents – but didn't name anyone or anything else.

"I'm talking about normal human behaviour. People who, people who hold positions of power, influence, and money don't want new kids on the block succeeding."

Let's be clear – it is a big claim to allege collusion between institutions or organisations collectively seeking to undermine him and his party, and there is no evidence for it.

But, crucially, you hear in his answer a sense of why he perceives that - that is what it feels like.

The question, as Reform's conference gets under way, is how the party approaches the coming days and the coming months.

Reform up against 'complainants' society', Farage tells BBC

"I've generally, you know, gone through politics with a smile…I'll go back to doing what I've been doing for the last 34 years," he said.

And as for their pitch to you at conference? A Reform government would achieve, and achieve quickly, they claim.

The party is promising a list of promises it would deliver in the first 100 days of a majority government, with every senior minister in a Farage government making and delivering one clear pledge.

But would they be able to if there is validity in their current claim that plenty of institutions are trying to stymie them?

Where does this unorthodox by-election victory leave Nigel Farage?

articles.title: Dutch central bank shifts billions in gold from US to Britain in ‘crisis preparedness’ move
articles.summary: The Dutch central bank announced Wednesday that it has moved billions of dollars worth of its gold reserves out of North America in a move it described as “crisis preparedness” in a time of global political unrest.
articles.body: The Dutch central bank announced Wednesday that it has moved billions of dollars worth of its gold reserves out of North America in a move it described as “crisis preparedness” in a time of global political unrest. It said that between March and August, some 86 metric tons (94.8 tons) of gold were transferred to London from the combined total of around 313 metric tons (345 tons) held in New York and Ottawa, Canada. Before the move, New York housed 31.3% of the Dutch gold and Ottawa held 19.7%. After the move, both cities now hold 18.5%, the bank said. The bank owns 612.4 metric tons (675 tons) of gold that was worth 72.2 billion euros (about $83.6 billion) at the end of 2025. “With this relocation, we have improved the tradability of our gold reserves,” the bank’s governor, Olaf Sleijpen, said in a written statement. “We expect that we will never need to use them, but we do need to strengthen our resilience and preparedness.” More than 27 metric tons (30 tons) of gold were “physically transferred” from the United States and Canada to the Dutch bank’s heavily guarded vault on a military base near the central town of Zeist, the bank said, without elaborating on exactly how the gold bars got across the Atlantic Ocean. A similar quantity of gold was transferred from Zeist to London. The rest of the relocation was achieved by selling around 59 metric tons (65 tons) of gold in New York and using the proceeds to buy gold in London. The Dutch bank, known by its acronym DNB, said that gold held at the Bank of England “must meet modern international trade standards and is regarded as the world’s most easily tradable gold and will therefore be the most readily available for DNB in a crisis situation. The gold reserves held in New York and Ottawa cannot be utilized as quickly and directly in such a situation.”

articles.title: Maine's high court gives father final say over daughter’s church attendance
articles.summary: The Maine Supreme Judicial Court upheld a father's authority over his daughter's attendance at an evangelical church after a pastor singled him out by name.
articles.body: The Maine Supreme Judicial Court affirmed a lower court ruling that granted a father final decision-making authority over whether his daughter attends her mother's evangelical church amid a parental dispute over the child's religious upbringing. The court's ruling on Tuesday maintains a Portland District Court judge's decision regarding a 2024 dispute between Matthew Bradeen and Emily Bickford about the church attendance of their daughter, who was 11 years old at the time, according to The Maine Monitor. Bickford had been taking her daughter to Calvary Chapel Greater Portland, an evangelical church in Westbrook, on multiple occasions each week. Bradeen argued the church was a "dangerous and harmful environment" that had caused anxiety in his daughter. He said she suffered a panic attack after hearing the church's teachings on the Rapture, a belief that Christians will suddenly be taken to heaven during the end times while nonbelievers will be left behind to face the apocalypse. NEW STUDY REVEALS THE SINGLE MOST CRITICAL FACTOR IN WHETHER CHILDREN KEEP THEIR FAITH INTO ADULTHOOD The lower court sided with Bradeen, finding that messages the child received at the church were "psychologically damaging" because of how it characterized her father, a ruling the state’s high court affirmed on Tuesday, according to The Maine Monitor. The lower court ruling granted Bradeen the right to decide whether his daughter attends services at Calvary Chapel, participates in church activities or interacts with church members other than her mother. The court also said the parents must "continue to share parental rights and responsibilities" when it comes to their daughter’s exposure to other religious groups. If the two disagreed on their daughter's religious exposure, the court ruled that the father has the final say. The court said the allocation of final decision-making authority stemmed from the parents' inability to jointly make decisions about the child's religious upbringing, not from disagreement with the mother's religious beliefs. Bickford’s lawyer, Mathew Staver, told The Maine Monitor he intends to appeal the case to the U.S. Supreme Court. Bickford and her legal team have 90 days to appeal the decision to the nation's highest court. Staver’s law firm, Liberty Counsel, which describes itself as a Christian ministry focused on religious freedom, has been involved in other religious freedom cases before the U.S. Supreme Court, including a 2022 case in which the court sided with a private religious group that Boston officials had prohibited from flying a Christian flag. In the dispute between Bradeen and Bickford, Liberty Counsel argued to Maine's high court that the 2024 order violated the mother's First Amendment rights through its "open hostility" toward religious beliefs and by barring her from influencing the "Religious upbringing of her child as she sees fit," the outlet reported. ORTHODOX JEW ASKS SUPREME COURT TO HEAR CASE AFTER CITY ALLEGEDLY TARGETED HIS HOME PRAYER GROUP "What Maine has done in this decision is put the Supreme Court of Maine at odds with the courts of a number of other states," Staver said. "I think it will be a case that will be very significant and catch the attention of the Supreme Court because of how far-reaching it is with regards to the First Amendment exercise clause." Bradeen's lawyer, Michelle King, called Tuesday's decision "well thought-out and reasoned," saying Bradeen was happy with the outcome, according to the outlet. "Anytime you’re in court, it’s stressful," King said. "But this case has definitely garnered a lot of media attention, and I think that’s always difficult for parents." Part of the case centered on a service in which the pastor singled out Bradeen by name, The Maine Monitor reported. As legal proceedings for the original dispute were ongoing, Bickford brought her daughter to a service at Calvary Chapel Greater Portland, where pastor Travis Carey led a six-and-a-half-minute prayer focused on the case, referring to the parents and child by name almost 30 times, saying Bradeen is "in need of salvation" and calling the proceedings "an attack on God's Word," according to the report. The Maine Supreme Court said Bickford did not make any attempt to pull her child from the service, and she later described it as "appropriate." Bickford "is unwilling to recognize, much less mitigate, the risk that these messages alienate the child from Bradeen or otherwise cause her harm," the court wrote. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In the 2024 lower court order, Maine District Court Judge Jennifer Nofsinger wrote that the harm caused to the daughter did not result from "a belief system that is rooted in the Bible," but rather, from the mother’s "inability to co-parent" regarding religion and the fact that she had given control of decisions about her daughter’s best interests to the church, and its language had denigrated the father. "The court found that the child was harmed by Bickford’s decisions to expose the child to messages that characterized Bradeen as an ‘enemy’ who seeks to ‘persecute’ the child and her faith, and by Bickford’s unwillingness to prevent the child from receiving those messages or to take any other steps to reduce the risk of alienating her from Bradeen," the Maine Supreme Court wrote in its decision on Tuesday upholding the lower court order. The final finding "reflected simply that it is harmful for a child to hear negative and frightening messages about one parent from the other parent or the other parent’s authority figures." The court ruled that the order was based on the parents’ inability to co-parent on religion, not on the substance of Bickford’s religious beliefs, finding it necessary for one parent to be given the power to make final decisions over the other.

articles.title: Mexican musician, pregnant wife, child and nanny killed in grisly shootings
articles.summary: A Mexican musician, his pregnant wife and 3-year-old daughter, as well as their nanny and a family dog were found dead on Tuesday, in a gruesome homicide case.
articles.body: A Mexican musician, his pregnant wife and 3-year-old daughter, as well as their nanny and a family dog were found dead on Tuesday, in a gruesome homicide case. Jonathan Meléndez, the 38-year-old keyboardist of the well-known indie rock band Camilo Séptimo, was among those found dead in an apartment in an upscale neighborhood near Mexico City late Tuesday night, the State of Mexico Attorney General’s Office said. His wife, Ana Paula, 35, was four months pregnant. The second woman’s family confirmed to reporters that the 21-year-old, named Aleida Romero Victorio, worked for the couple as a nanny. “She was a very hardworking and responsible girl who did not deserve for this to be done to her,” said her aunt, Lorena Victorio Cabrera. Three of the victims – including the young girl – were shot in the head, authorities said, while the other was shot in the back. “Two of the victims were found with their hands bound,” the prosecutor’s office said. The dog was found dead, with its legs tied. A 6-year-old boy was found alive at the scene and was unharmed, they added. Authorities believe the killings occurred between 5:30 p.m. and 7:40 p.m. on Tuesday. Meléndez’s band said he would be remembered “with immense love and gratitude.” “Today we honor and celebrate his life, his music, his light, and what he shared with those of us fortunate enough to know him and walk alongside him,” Camilo Séptimo said on Instagram. Two men were arrested in connection with the deaths on Wednesday, in a joint operation involving the State of Mexico Prosecutor’s Office, the federal Secretariat of Security and Citizen Protection and the Mexico City Secretariat of Citizen Security. An associate of Meléndez, identified as Diego Sebastián “N,” is accused of being the probable perpetrator, the prosecutor’s office said. Another man identified as Gerardo “N” is also under investigation for his alleged involvement. CNN is trying to determine if the detainees have legal representation. One of the suspects allegedly “exploited” his relationship with one of the victims to enter the home, according to Omar García Harfuch, Mexico’s secretary of security and citizen protection. The prosecutor’s office said it would disclose the circumstances of the killings and the legal status of the detainees at the appropriate procedural stage.

articles.title: UK mortgage approvals fall to lowest level since January 2024 as housing demand weakens
articles.summary: News News: Mortgage approvals for house purchases in the UK fell to their lowest level since January 2024 in July, signalling weaker demand in the housing market.
articles.body: Mortgage approvals for house purchases in the UK fell to their lowest level since January 2024 in July, signalling weaker demand in the housing market as borrowing costs continue to weigh on prospective buyers.According to Reuters, citing Bank of England data, lenders approved 56,053 mortgages for house purchases in July, down from 58,215 in June and below the 59,500 median forecast in a Reuters poll of economists. The figure was also well below the six-month average of around 60,800.Higher mortgage costs weigh on buyersThe decline in approvals points to softer housing activity in the months ahead, as mortgage approvals are an important indicator of future property transactions. The figures suggest buyers remain cautious despite modest growth in house prices.Net mortgage borrowing dropped sharply to £4.3 billion in July from £7.7 billion in June, falling below the previous six-month average of £5.3 billion. Gross mortgage lending also declined to £25.9 billion from £26.9 billion.Higher borrowing costs remain a major challenge for buyers. The effective interest rate on newly drawn mortgages rose to 4.45 percent in July from 4.35 percent in June, while the rate on outstanding mortgages edged up to 3.97 percent from 3.96 percent.House prices face pressure as demand slowsThe weakness in mortgage demand comes as house prices continue to record modest annual growth. Nationwide said UK house prices rose 1.6 percent in the year to August, according to Reuters. However, the increase was below consumer price inflation, meaning house prices declined in inflation-adjusted terms.The broader borrowing picture was mixed. Unsecured consumer borrowing increased by about £2 billion in July, above economists' expectations and the highest monthly rise since November 2025. This suggests households continued to rely on credit for spending even as demand for housing finance weakened.The Bank of England's interest-rate outlook will remain crucial for the property market. The central bank's policy rate stands at 3.75 percent, while markets have been pricing in a possible 25-basis-point increase by the end of the year.For the UK housing market, weaker mortgage approvals combined with elevated borrowing costs could keep transactions subdued. If the decline in approvals persists, it could also put further pressure on house-price growth as buyers continue to face affordability constraints.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Rusty state of USS Abraham Lincoln after marathon deployment shocks observers
articles.summary: As the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln pulled into port in Thailand on Wednesday, observers were shocked by its appearance. The almost 1,100-foot-long warship was covered in rust from bow to stern.
articles.body: As the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln pulled into port in Thailand on Wednesday, observers were shocked by its appearance. The almost 1,100-foot-long warship was covered in rust from bow to stern. But experts say that’s to be expected from what the Navy says was 286 days at sea since the Lincoln left its homeport of San Diego last November. The warship also saw months of combat and blockade operations against Iran in the Middle East. “Rust along the waterline is not unusual on a ship that has spent 60 days or more of operations continuously at sea,” said Carl Schuster, a former US Navy captain who did three tours on Nimitz-class carriers like the Lincoln. Tackling the rust problem is not something that could be done at sea, especially during combat operations, Schuster told CNN. Crews would need to be lowered down to the waterline, sand off the rust, put on two coats of rust-preventative primer and then two coats of naval gray paint, according to Schuster. “Based on what I am seeing, you are looking at about 30 days of preservation work to remove all the rust,” he said. Some work might be done on critical areas during the stop in Thailand, Schuster added. The Lincoln docked in the port of Laem Chabang, on the Gulf of Thailand, south of Bangkok, on Wednesday for a visit expected to last several days to give crew members their first full rest-and-relaxation port call after a marathon deployment. “They will do only high-priority work during a seven-day port visit. The rust on the bow and forward hull areas will done first because they take the most abuse when the ship is moving, and they absorb the corrosive actions that accompany moving through salt waters, particularly choppy seas,” Schuster said. Some of the rust on upper levels can be treated while the ship is underway, but it must be stationary and free from wave action when making the repairs along the waterline, he said. But it is a problem that can’t be neglected. “Rust is like a contagious disease. It spreads. So, it is better to deal with it early to contain it or deal with a much larger problem later,” Schuster said. “It weakens any steel structure it attacks. So, you have to remove it before it has a decisive impact on your components” like decks, walkways and lifelines, he said. Rust hasn’t been the only problem associated with the Lincoln’s long deployment. It has led to reports of morale problems amid supply shortages, and at least one crew member going overboard. But US President Donald Trump has dismissed concerns, saying the Lincoln’s deployment was “not nearly long enough.” No comment on the condition of the Lincoln has been heard from Trump since it arrived in Thailand. But in the past, the US president has called for the Navy to clean up the appearance of its warships, which have been facing longer deployments in his second administration. Last year, then-Navy Secretary John Phelan said Trump would call him in the middle of the night about the rust problem. “He has stated to me many times: ‘Shipbuilding, shipbuilding, shipbuilding. Get those ships out of maintenance yards. Fix the damn rust,’” Phelan said at a conference in Maryland, as reported by Task & Purpose. “He does not like it, and I don’t like getting calls in the middle of the night.” It’s not something sailors like either, said Schuster. “Fighting rust is one of the two most unpopular naval activities. The other being anything to do with plumbing. Hated both as a junior officer on a ship.”

articles.body: KOLKATA: Dramatic visuals purportedly from the Trinamool Congress' Camac Street office in Kolkata showed several masked and helmeted men walking out of the premises carrying TV screens, a printer and other items after an alleged early-morning attack on Thursday.The footage also showed a room littered with broken objects, with furniture and electronic equipment apparently damaged.TMC national general secretary Abhishek Banerjee alleged that BJP workers, armed with weapons, stormed the party office at around 4.30am, assaulted people inside, snatched their phones, smashed furniture and ransacked the premises.Calling it a "disgraceful assault on the rule of law", Banerjee alleged that Kolkata Police failed to respond for nearly two hours despite repeated calls and emails from party workers and lawyers."We demand the immediate arrest of every person involved in this attack," Banerjee said, while also seeking an investigation into who allegedly planned, organised and directed the violence and accountability for the alleged police inaction.Following the incident, the Trinamool Congress wrote to President Droupadi Murmu and West Bengal Governor RN Ravi seeking urgent appointments with party delegations to discuss what it described as the "disturbing and systematic misuse" of the police and the deteriorating law-and-order situation in the state.Speaking to reporters, TMC MP Derek O'Brien said the letters were sent on Thursday morning and sought separate meetings with the President in Delhi and the West Bengal Governor in Kolkata."In this situation, we've written to the President of India, and the Trinamool Congress has written to the Governor of West Bengal — President and the Governor — seeking an urgent appointment of a Trinamool Congress delegation to discuss the disturbing situation in Bengal," O'Brien said.The TMC alleged that the incident at the Camac Street office was part of a wider deterioration in law and order and demanded action against those responsible.The BJP, however, rejected the allegations of political vendetta.Responding to Abhishek Banerjee's posts, West Bengal BJP president Samik Bhattacharya said the BJP would not have spared defeated TMC leaders if it were pursuing vendetta politics."If the BJP were engaging in vendetta politics, then after the election results were declared, none of the defeated Trinamool Congress MLAs, ministers and MPs would have remained unscathed," Bhattacharya said.He also alleged that internal differences within the TMC were responsible for incidents of violence and vandalism."Trinamool members are throwing eggs at each other and vandalising each other's offices. Those who faced injustice at the hands of Abhishek Banerjee, when he was a top party leader, understand the situation," he said.The incident comes amid an ongoing controversy over Banerjee's Camac Street office. articles.title: US medical groups issue vaccine guidance, urge jabs for flu, COVID and RSV
articles.summary: Top medical groups say current evidence shows these vaccines protect against severe illness and death.
articles.body:
A coalition of leading medical groups in the United States has urged the public to get updated vaccinations for influenza and COVID-19, publishing its own guidance to fill a gap left by shifting advice from the federal government.

The coalition, which includes the American Medical Association (AMA) and American Academy of Pediatrics, issued the vaccine guidance for respiratory illnesses on Wednesday.

It included the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and varied by age group and other factors, such as pregnancy.

“The latest high-quality scientific evidence found that these immunisations continue to provide meaningful protection against severe illness, hospitalisation and death,” the groups said in a statement.

The coalition said it hoped to ease “confusion and chaos” caused by the absence of updated vaccine recommendations, and noted that recent scientific studies have raised no new health concerns related to vaccines for the viruses.

“Patients need and deserve vaccine recommendations that are clear, credible, and based on the best available scientific evidence, so they can make informed vaccine decisions for themselves and for their families,” AMA president-elect Sandra Fryhofer told a news conference.

She said the coalition’s independent review has been published online so “the public has clear, consistent, science-based guidance even while the federal process is in flux”.

The advice usually comes from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), with help from its independent advisers. But the administration of President Donald Trump, in a sweeping overhaul of vaccine policy, began last year pulling back on some longstanding recommendations for virus protection and routine children’s vaccinations.

These include recommendations for the hepatitis B vaccine for newborns and the COVID-19 vaccine for US residents older than six months.

Medical associations repeatedly vocally opposed steps taken under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who is a vaccine sceptic, and said the changes run counter to scientific consensus.

A federal judge has since suspended many of the administration’s measures, ruling in March that the federal government had disregarded science-based methods. That decision has hampered the work of the expert panel advising the CDC on vaccination recommendations.

This year, the federal government has only issued guidance for influenza, or the flu, extending its advice from last year.

The guidance from the medical groups on Wednesday recommended an annual influenza shot for everyone six months and older, as well as updated COVID vaccines for healthy adults, young children and pregnant women. It also advised RSV immunisations for older adults, pregnant women and children younger than eight months.

Influenza had the highest burden of the three during the 2025-2026 respiratory virus season, with about 32 million to 52 million cases, 390,000 hospitalisations and 24,000 deaths in the US, according to CDC estimates.

There were about 4.6 million to 12.9 million COVID cases over the same period, with 140,000 to 240,000 hospitalisations and 15,000 to 42,000 deaths, according to CDC preliminary estimates .

RSV caused an estimated 2.8 million to 5.8 million outpatient visits, 170,000 to 340,000 hospitalisations, and up to 25,000 deaths.

The burden of influenza and COVID declined in the 2025-2026 season compared with the previous year, while RSV activity remained relatively similar.

articles.title: How can Bengaluru build its way out of traffic?
articles.summary: Bengaluru’s proposed tunnel road has brought an old question back into focus: can the city actually build its way out of its traffic mess? The answer .
articles.body: Bengaluru’s proposed tunnel road has brought an old question back into focus: can the city actually build its way out of its traffic mess? The answer is unlikely to come from one mega project. Tunnels, flyovers and wider roads can ease congestion on particular stretches, but the relief may not last if the number of vehicles keeps climbing. What Bengaluru needs is a transport system that makes it easier for people to leave their cars at home, while also making better use of the roads it already has.The tunnel roadThe attraction of a tunnel road is easy to understand. It can take traffic below some of the city's busiest roads, bypass crowded junctions and create a new route without requiring large-scale land acquisition on the surface.But there is a catch. Traffic does not end when a tunnel ends. If thousands of vehicles emerge onto a road that is already struggling to cope, the congestion could simply move a few kilometres down the road. The success of the project will therefore depend as much on how it connects with the existing road network as on the tunnel itself.Chief minister DK Shivakumar has argued that widening existing roads is difficult because much of Bengaluru was not planned for its present scale. He has also pointed to the city’s rapid growth and rising vehicle numbers as reasons why new mobility infrastructure is needed.Have more roads really solved the problem?Bengaluru has tried the road-building approach before. Flyovers, road widening and elevated corridors have all been presented as ways to tackle specific congestion points. Some have certainly helped traffic move better for a period.But the city has also seen a familiar pattern: a new stretch opens, traffic improves, vehicle numbers rise and congestion returns. More road space can make driving more convenient, which in turn can encourage more people to use cars. This makes road construction a race that becomes harder to win every year.Bengaluru's problem is bigger than roadsThe city's traffic problem is also a consequence of how Bengaluru has grown. Large employment centres have emerged in particular parts of the city, while housing has spread much farther out. The result is millions of people travelling long distances, often at roughly the same time every day.Then there are the smaller problems that add up: badly designed junctions, parking on busy roads, construction work, narrow stretches and poor last-mile connections. Fixing one road cannot solve all of these at once.Metro can move more people, not just more carsThis is where public transport becomes crucial. Bengaluru's expanding Metro network can carry vastly more people through a corridor than private cars can. But a Metro station is useful only if commuters can get to it easily and complete the rest of their journey without too much hassle.Better feeder buses, autos, walking routes and safe pedestrian access are therefore just as important as adding new Metro lines. For many commuters, the decision to use public transport comes down to convenience. If reaching the station is difficult, the car remains the easier option.The bus that is stuck in trafficBuses can make an even bigger difference because they already serve a large section of the city's commuters. The problem is that BMTC buses are often caught in the same traffic as everyone else.Dedicated bus lanes, better routes, more frequent services and signal priority could help buses carry more people without requiring another major road project. On a crowded Bengaluru road, a lane carrying dozens of people in a bus is arguably more valuable than a lane carrying a handful of cars.Don't just fix roads — fix bottlenecksOne of Bengaluru's biggest challenges is that traffic rarely stops at one location. A project may clear a junction only for vehicles to queue up at the next one.That means the city needs to look at entire corridors rather than individual trouble spots. Sometimes a redesigned junction, a better signal system or the removal of a particular bottleneck can make a bigger difference than kilometres of new road.Technology can unlock existing capacityThere is also plenty that Bengaluru can do without digging up another road. Traffic signals can be coordinated more intelligently. Real-time data can be used to manage congestion. Parking can be better regulated and enforcement can be strengthened.None of these measures has the glamour of a tunnel or flyover. But they can often be introduced faster and at a fraction of the cost, while making the existing network work more efficiently.The cost of building moreBig infrastructure projects are expensive, and tunnel construction brings its own technical and financial challenges. There is also the disruption that comes with years of construction.That does not automatically make the tunnel road a bad idea. Bengaluru may well need new road capacity in some places. But every major investment should be judged against alternatives. Could the same money move more people if it went into Metro connectivity, bus lanes, pedestrian infrastructure or last-mile services?The important question is not simply how many vehicles a project can accommodate. It is how many people it can move, and how reliably.Build for people, not just vehiclesThis may be the most important shift Bengaluru needs to make. The city cannot keep expanding road capacity at the same pace as vehicle ownership.So, yes, Bengaluru may have to build its way out of traffic. But building should not mean only pouring more concrete or digging more tunnels. It should mean building a transport network in which Metro, buses, roads, walking and cycling complement one another.The real measure of successThe tunnel road should ultimately be judged on more than whether cars can travel faster through a particular corridor. The bigger test is whether it helps people get across Bengaluru more quickly and reliably.If success is measured by how many cars a road can carry, the city could remain trapped in a never-ending cycle of expansion and congestion. But if the goal is to move more people with fewer vehicles, the solution becomes much broader.Bengaluru's traffic crisis will probably not be solved by a single tunnel, flyover or road. articles.title: Channel smuggling gangs resort to 'mega-dinghies' as crackdown limits small boat supply
articles.summary: Once-rival criminal groups are being forced to work together because of a shortage of small boats, a BBC investigation has found.
articles.body:
A drop in small boats illegally reaching the UK is forcing people smuggling gangs to adopt new tactics, a BBC investigation has found.

And there are claims of more "mega-dinghies" being prepared, of the type seen arriving on UK shores in recent weeks.

The image of a 15-metre long small boat carrying a record 230 migrants towards the UK drew condemnation from both newspapers and politicians.

Ministers were accused of "losing control" of illegal Channel crossings, and the French police again found themselves criticised for not intervening.

But evocative as the picture was, it also represented a new strategy by the increasingly frustrated people smugglers we encountered on France's northern shores - who attacked our crew with stones, and injured our cameraman.

They are running low on small boats, we have found. And once rival criminal groups are now having to work together by loading more migrants on fewer, larger vessels - just like the "mega dinghy".

The UK and France are announcing measures to increase the number of police officers on the French coast in order to try to stop the migrants.

The latest initiative comes as Andy Burnham prepares to host French President Emmanuel Macron at Downing Street for the first time since becoming prime minister.

Gang members have told our sources that others are being prepared, to the concern of emergency teams on both sides of the Channel, because of the increased risk to more lives. On 4 August 170 people had to be rescued after theirs caught fire in the middle of the Channel.

With French officers claiming they are now intercepting two-thirds of small boats before they can reach the coast, that means fewer crossing opportunities. And for those hoping to make the journey, it means a higher price.

Today, the gangs are quoting up to €2,000 (£1,700) per person. It used to be around €1,300 just a year ago. Their passengers also have to now pay in cash, to ensure commitment.

During one early low tide on Gravelines beach, we saw the only small boat to launch that day, and it was not what we expected.

At 09:30, a dozen or so migrants emerged from the sand dunes. Their distinctive orange life jackets, purchased from a local sports shop, made them easy to identify.

A need for speed at this point would be a fair assumption, but this was not to be the case. There was no running. It was almost orderly. A refined process where instructions were obeyed.

As they waded into the calm shallows of the Channel, their "taxi boat" came into view. It is simply a small boat that has departed from further along the coastline to avoid detection. Only now, they are being forced to set off from even greater distances. This one had left from Belgium.

The reason for the group not rushing was because the boat was already in the water. French police argue they are prevented from intervening at this point over fears of people drowning. It is to the long frustration of the British authorities, who would like their neighbours to at least adopt a more "case-by-case" approach.

As they clutch their phones in plastic wrapping, the group patiently waits for what they hope will be a voyage to a better life in the UK. Some tell me they are from Afghanistan. They are eager to catch their ride. Those who make it on are visibly elated.

After the last passenger, a young boy, is almost thrown on board, it inches out to sea, but it is not leaving yet.

At 09:49, another group of migrants move into the water and wait to be collected. An hour later, the boat indeed does return, but to another gathering that has emerged on a different part of the beach. A few run the vast distance across the sand to try to secure a spot. Most manage to clamber on.

As police officers watch from the shore, the small boat goes on to make five collections like this over three hours. The boarding becomes more frantic as the window of opportunity shrinks.

By 12:11, the small boat, with 82 people on board, finally moves off into the busiest shipping lane in the world. It is dwarfed by the passenger ferries in the background.

Everyone successfully made it to the UK. Small boats typically radio for help once they are in British waters, as the coastguard is compelled to rescue them and take them to shore.

What they leave behind in Gravelines is a scene of dejection and exhaustion. A limp toddler is carried past me towards a police officer, who revives him with a light shake.

This all unfolds next to four or so men casting their fishing rods into the increasingly choppy waters. It is peak holiday season here. They and other dogwalkers barely glance at the crestfallen migrants wading back to the sand.

Before, the gangs would often launch boats in the dead of night, but with increased police patrols, charity workers tell us the gangs now see the middle of the day as a better opportunity, as it takes taxi boats longer to arrive and it allows them to better co-ordinate boarding.

"You feel guilty being there - going to the beach and having a good time, while these families are in such terrible situations," observes a woman with her young daughter. They had been playing with a bucket and spade.

"It's hard," she admits. "We regularly see people on the beach attempting the crossing. It feels like living in two parallel worlds that have nothing to do with each other; it's really strange."

The migrants remaining will wait for their next opportunity, as per their agreement with the gangs. But because of more robust policing that wait is now typically weeks, even months, rather than days.

They also need a favourable weather window: the wind needs to ideally be under 5 knots and waves need to be less than 0.8m for a small boat to have a chance of making it across.

To improve their chances of avoiding detection and to be closer to a taxi boat, charity workers tell us migrants are also sleeping closer to the beach in the woods or among the dunes, instead of at the larger camps where they can wash, or receive food, water and medication.

It is after arriving at the largest settlement at Loon-Plage, near Dunkirk, that we soon find ourselves in direct confrontation with the people smugglers.

As the intense heat bears down on a tent where people can charge their devices, we initially meet two young Egyptian men who are visibly tired and disheartened. They have been staying in squalid conditions for months and have made several unsuccessful attempts to cross.

"The police stopped us from leaving and destroyed the boats," explains one. He says he wants to go to the UK so he can work and obtain legal papers.

A young Sudanese woman and Afghan man also told us they had also tried to cross dozens of times. We have been to the camp on several occasions over the past year, but this time there was a perceptible unease.

Riot police had cleared out the tents in the same week, and the day before around 400 migrants preparing for a taxi boat in the nearby Hardelot forest were forced to return after several fires broke out.

It is evident the migrants and the gangs have been repeatedly frustrated, and the sight of our camera in one corner of the camp leads to us being attacked.

After agreeing to stop filming, one smuggler, around 5'8" tall (172cm) and in a new grey tracksuit, tries to grab our camera. He then repeatedly throws rocks at us from close range, striking our cameraman above the eye.

We're chased to the car and make it away. Pol would later receive a few stitches.

The UK has been quick to praise the French police for reducing crossing numbers to a six-year low. Officials also cite a deeper, more coordinated level of coordination between the two countries.

But changes in immigration policy, the movement of people and the weather means the broader picture is more complicated.

Thousands are still illegally entering the UK every month on small boats. The numbers remain significant. And motivations to make this journey still run deep in this stretch of northern France.

For the people smuggling gangs that still means money, and a need to evolve.

Additional reporting by Marianne Baisnée

articles.title: Tamil for Madras HC: CM Vijay to move resolution urging Centre's approval
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay is set to move a resolution in the state assembly on Thursday urging the Centre to recognise Tamil.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay is set to move a resolution in the state assembly on Thursday urging the Centre to recognise Tamil as the principal language of the Madras high court, official sources said.The resolution will be moved by Vijay during the assembly session and is likely to be taken up for discussion. It will seek a formal framework to ensure that judgments, decrees and judicial orders of the high court are also made available in Tamil.The move is expected to highlight Tamil's status as a classical language. It will also point to the significant development of legal terminology in Tamil. The resolution is likely to cite technology-enabled translation facilities as another factor supporting the proposal.The state government will also refer to the existing legal provisions governing the use of regional languages in high court proceedings and judgments. Under the current framework, a state's official language can be used in addition to English, but this requires the Governor's authorisation and the prior consent of the President.The resolution is also expected to recall an earlier attempt by the Tamil Nadu assembly. On December 6, 2006, the House had passed a resolution seeking the use of Tamil in the Madras high court. The resolution was subsequently forwarded to the Union government.The latest proposal seeks to revive the demand and push for Tamil to be recognised as the principal language of the Madras high court.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: MoD withheld information about nuclear test veterans' records, ex-minister claims
articles.summary: Cold War veterans who oversaw nuclear tests have claimed they caused lifelong health problems.
articles.body:
Former veterans minister Tobias Ellwood has said the Ministry of Defence (MoD) deliberately withheld information about the medical records of Cold War veterans who oversaw nuclear tests.

Ellwood told BBC Newsnight he now believes some information he gave to Parliament about the UK's nuclear programme, based on MoD briefings, was "a complete lie".

Veterans have campaigned for the release of their medical histories, arguing blood and urine test results could help them prove that nuclear exposure damaged their health.

An MoD spokesperson said the government had conducted an "extensive records discovery exercise" to address questions about the programme, with its findings published in full.

As many as 25,000 members of the UK armed services, scientists and civilians took part in the nuclear testing programme between 1952 and 1967 at sites including Australia and several islands in the Pacific Ocean.

Veterans have claimed the tests caused severe lifelong health problems, alleging they have suffered cancers of the liver, bone, bowel, skin and brain, as well as leukaemia, heart disease, stillbirths and generational birth defects as a result of their exposure.

Ellwood, who served as a junior defence minister between June 2017 and July 2019, says he believes ministers over the years have been briefed to say they had no evidence to help nuclear test veterans, as part of an effort to delay until they have passed away.

He said the ministry "deliberately withheld" information about the testing programme.

"The more you unpick this story, the more murky, the more shady, the concerning it becomes," Ellwood told Newsnight.

The MoD in 2024 promised to embark on a comprehensive examination of any information the department holds on the issue, and has since released five reports.

In those, it said there were a number of factors affecting the way medical records were kept, including the lack of a centralised approach and high levels of Cold War "secrecy".

An MoD spokesperson said the government had examined "tens of thousands of documents to address long-standing questions from veterans about blood and urine testing policies during the nuclear testing programme".

They said it had been published in its entirety "following regular engagement between Ministers, nuclear test veterans and community groups throughout the process."

"We owe an enduring debt of gratitude to the more than 22,000 Service personnel, scientists and civilians who contributed to the UK's nuclear testing programme and helped safeguard our national security," the spokesperson said.

articles.title: George Michael's  'Faith' guitar to be auctioned
articles.summary: The guitar he played in the Faith video is part of a collection belonging to his PA
articles.body:
The guitar played by George Michael in the music video for Faith is expected to fetch £100,000 at auction.

The song was the title track of the Hertfordshire pop star's 1987 debut solo album, which sold more than 25 million copies worldwide.

In the video, the former Wham! frontman wore a leather jacket and aviator sunglasses while playing the guitar, as part of an attempt to reinvent his image.

Auction House, Sworders, is putting the guitar under the hammer on 29 October, along with other items from the collection of his personal assistant, Siobhan Bailey, who died in 2014.

The collection features itineraries from Wham! and George Michael tours, including their 1985 visit to China , estimated to sell for between £300 and £600.

A gold disc celebrating 500,000 UK sales of Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go is estimated to sell for at least £200.

The complete archive is expected to sell for more than £200,000.

Guy Schooling, chairman of Sworders, described the Faith guitar as the "jewel in the crown" of the collection.

He said: "The sale will offer avid fans around the globe, the chance to own not just pieces of music history, but objects that capture the spirit and ambition of one of pop's greatest and most-loved artists."

Earlier this year, the leather jacket Michael wore in the Faith video sold for £176,400 at an auction run by Hertfordshire-based Propstore.

The Ray-Ban sunglasses he wore on stage during the 1988 Faith Tour will be offered by Propstore in a two-day auction beginning on 1 October. They are expected to fetch at least £15,000.
